title: How Requests Are Reviewed
leaves: Every request gets an answer within five business days.
run: The week before the first weekly triage. It can start before the first quarter, and it is the fastest visible win.

slides.html:
Practice training

How requests are reviewed

Triage, small requests, and the idea log. How every request gets an answer, and how the roadmap stays focused on goals.
slides.notes: Built from an earlier version of this flow, drawn for a ServiceNow team (How are my requests reviewed and categorized? and the small request frames), and doc 08. This version follows the current system.

slides.html:
Where we are, and where we want to be

What it feels like today

  • "I sent a request and never heard back."
  • So the next ask comes as a hallway conversation, an email to a manager, or a call to someone who knows someone.
  • The team gets pulled in every direction, and the loudest ask wins.
  • Big ideas and small fixes sit in the same pile, and both wait.

Where we want to be

  • Every request gets an outcome within 5 business days, and the requester is told.
  • Small fixes get done, from a protected share of our time.
  • Big ideas are kept, and looked at when we plan.
  • The roadmap stays focused on goals.
slides.notes: Start with the requester's experience, not the process. Most people in the room have been on both sides: the person waiting and the person getting the hallway ask.

slides.notes: Same shape as the earlier flow. One change: "Already on the roadmap" is now its own outcome, so nothing that is already planned gets logged a second time.

slides.html:
Five outcomes, five tests

Already on the roadmap

The roadmap already covers it as an Initiative, Solution, or Deliverable.

Small request

A request to alter an existing functionality or item that can be completed in less than a single sprint.

Large or strategic

A request to either add new functionality or a request that will take longer than a single sprint.

Idea for improvement

A request to make the overall system better that would have impacts to people or groups beyond the requester.

Will not do

A request that cannot be accommodated for either feasibility, cost, or strategic reasons.

Improvement or small? Ideas for improvement stay separate because at triage we don't know their size. If it's a clear, bounded fix to something that exists, call it a small request even if others benefit.
slides.notes: The four definitions from the earlier flow are kept word for word. "Already on the roadmap" is new.

slides.html:
Who is in the room

A 30 to 45 minute weekly meeting. Every request since the last review gets an outcome.

Product owner

Runs the review. Owns the small request board and steps in when its order needs to change. Sends or delegates each reply.

Product manager

Owns the idea log. Calls "already on the roadmap" and "will not do" for strategy reasons. Mines the log for patterns.

Content strategist

Brings requests from editors and partners, explains the context, and argues for the ones that matter most to them.

Technical architect or developer

Flags anything that may be infeasible or bigger than it looks.

Requesters

Don't attend. They get a reply.

Not here: scoring

No weighted models or 2x2s at triage. Those help compare large candidates at quarterly planning.
slides.notes: If the team has no content strategist, the product owner brings partner requests. Keep the meeting short; if a request needs a long discussion, it is probably large or strategic.

slides.html:
Bugs skip triage

A bug is something we built that doesn't work as intended. Nobody is asking for a change.

Bug reported

→

Technical architect

→

Stops people using the service, exposes data, or opens a security hole

→

Fix it now

Everything else

→

Technical maintenance list, in priority order

It counts as Technical maintenance

Bugs are paid for from Technical maintenance time, not small request time, whoever reported them.

Unless it isn't a bug

If a "bug" is really a request for different behavior, send it back to triage.
slides.notes: DMV example: "Renewal payments over $500 fail at the last step." It blocks people from finishing, so the technical architect had it fixed that day.

slides.html:
Every request gets an answer

Set expectations, and explain any no and why.

Already on the roadmap

"This is already part of [roadmap item]. You can follow progress here."

Small request

"This is on our small request board. We work these in the order they arrive, unless something is urgent, and expect to get to it within [typical time]. We'll tell you when it's done."

Large or strategic

"This is bigger than a quick fix, so we've added it to our idea log. We review the log every quarter when we plan. We can't promise a date."

Idea for improvement

"This could help more people than the original ask, so we've logged it as an improvement idea. We'll look at it more closely when we plan next quarter."

Will not do

"We won't be taking this on because [reason]." Plus an alternative, if there is one.

A no with a reason builds more trust than silence. If nobody hears back, the next request goes around the system as a hallway ask.
slides.notes: Full reply templates are in doc 08. Each starts with "Thanks."

slides.html:
Future consideration: not yes, not no

Some ideas are worth keeping but don't fit our strategy or capacity now, and nothing tells us when they will. After the product manager reviews an idea, this status tells the requester three things plainly:

We aren't saying yes

We aren't saying no

We won't get back to you

The idea stays in the log. If it fits a future quarter, the product manager will find it there. The requester can always ask again, especially if something changes on their side.

Why it exists

The alternative is silence. People read silence as a forgotten yes or a quiet no, so they keep waiting or keep asking.

Saying "we won't follow up" once is kinder than leaving them to guess.
slides.notes: DMV example: a deputy director asked for a chatbot that answers renewal questions. At Q2 planning the product manager marked it Future consideration: the renewal service and its help content are still changing, so a chatbot built now would be out of date in weeks. The reply said so, and that the team won't follow up.

slides.html:
Large requests get a conversation

Most arrive as a solution with a deadline attached: "we need a portal by July."

1

Is the problem clear, rather than a solution?

Ask what happens today, who it affects, and what goes wrong. If nobody can say, the first step is discovery.

2

Is there a hard deadline?

Separate a mandate (law, policy, funding) from a wish. A real mandate makes it Required work, which still competes at planning.

3

Do we need more discovery?

If the problem is real but unclear, it becomes a discovery candidate for planning.

4

Can the scope be reduced?

Sometimes a smaller version solves most of the problem and fits as a small request now.

5

Does the partner understand how we work?

Explain the quarterly cycle: what can happen now, what waits for planning, and when they will hear.

The partner leaves knowing what happens next and when they will hear. The outcome: a planning candidate, Required work, a small request, Future consideration, or will not do.
slides.notes: The product manager meets the requester before the idea goes in the log, with the UX designer and researcher if possible. The problem underneath is usually smaller or different.

slides.html:
Example: a portal for oversize load permits by July

DMV Motor Carrier unit. The product manager met the unit lead with the UX designer and researcher.

1. Problem

Carriers fax applications, and a third come back for missing route details. The problem is rework, not the lack of a portal.

2. Deadline

July is the start of construction season. A wish, not a mandate.

3. Discovery

Needed. Nobody knows which route details go missing or why.

4. Reduced scope

A fillable route checklist on the existing permits page fits as a small request now.

5. How we work

The lead heard that a portal would be considered at Q3 planning at the earliest.

Small request board

The fillable route checklist.

Idea log

"Carriers resubmit oversize permits," as a discovery candidate for Q3 planning.
slides.notes: The original ask: "an online portal for oversize load permits by July." One request, two outcomes. The partner got something useful now and an honest answer about the rest.

slides.html:
How does small request work get prioritized and scheduled?

Ready

first in, first out

Route checklist on the permits page

Title transfer fee table

Holiday hours banner

In sprint

pulled this sprint

Sticker arrival date on the renewal confirmation

Done

 

Address change link on the renewal start page

Requester told

 

New study guide link on the test page

A capacity share, not roadmap work

Small requests get a fixed share of team time, 25% by default, set each quarter. "It's not a road mapping activity."

First in, first out

Requests are pulled in the order they arrived. Urgency can move one up, and the product owner can step in to reorder.

Patterns go up, requests stay put

When several small requests point to the same problem, add that pattern to the idea log.
slides.notes: Cards are DMV examples: the sticker request from the Jan 21 triage, the route checklist from the Motor Carrier intake conversation, the address-change link from week 1. The rest are illustrative. Change from the earlier flow: in the ServiceNow version, catalog owners and steering ordered small requests. In the system, the board runs first in, first out; urgency can move a request up, and the product owner owns the share and steps in to change the order. The product manager doesn't plan small requests. If the product manager is ordering the small request board, it has turned into a second roadmap.

slides.html:
How does the team balance its work?

Product manager

orders

Strategic

Roadmap Initiatives and Deliverables

50% of team time

Product owner

orders

Small requests

From triage, first in, first out

25% of team time

Technical architect

orders

Technical maintenance

Including bugs, in priority order

25% of team time

Triage feeds two of the three. Small requests go to the product owner's board. Large and strategic ideas go to the product manager's idea log, which feeds the roadmap at planning. The split is set each quarter.
slides.notes: Same three lanes as the earlier flow, with today's owners and names. The defaults are 50/25/25 and change by quarter.

slides.html:
The idea log is a toy chest, not a queue

Logging promises one thing

That the idea won't get lost. No commitment, no date, no place in line.

The product manager mines it

At quarterly planning, for candidates to frame as Initiatives. At direction setting, for patterns that might shape strategy.

Most ideas never become Initiatives

And that is expected. Each one moves from Needs review to Mined into an Initiative, Future consideration, or Closed.

Triage is where requests come in. Planning is where the ideas get used.

Log ideas freely and promise nothing. Nobody should read "logged" as "scheduled."
slides.notes: DMV example: a counter clerk's idea, "show a document checklist before someone comes in for a new license," was logged in January and mined into the Initiative "Single-trip new driver licenses" at Q2 planning.

slides.html:
Try it: a DMV triage review

Tuesday, January 21. Give each request one of the five outcomes.

"Can people renew their registration online yet?"

Field office manager

?

"The renewal confirmation page doesn't say when the sticker arrives."

Call center lead

?

"Let people book a knowledge test appointment online."

Public comment

?

"Show a document checklist before someone comes in for a new license."

Counter clerk

?

"Turn the paper renewal form into a fillable PDF."

Records unit

?

Outcomes: Already on the roadmap, Small request, Large or strategic, Idea for improvement, Will not do.
slides.notes: Give the room two minutes in pairs. The interesting arguments are usually 3 versus 4, and whether 5 is a no or an idea.

Tuesday, January 21.

"The renewal confirmation page doesn't say when the sticker arrives."

Call center lead

Small request: added to the board

"Let people book a knowledge test appointment online."

Public comment

Counter clerk

Idea for improvement: idea log, tagged to Goal 2

"Turn the paper renewal form into a fillable PDF."

Records unit

Will not do: we will not digitize existing broken processes

The no came with a reason and a path: "Our strategy is to redesign renewal end to end rather than put the old form online, and the online renewal service is already in progress. Here is where to follow it."
slides.notes: The sticker request was pulled into the next sprint against the 2-week small request response commitment. The checklist idea was tagged to Goal 2, zero multi-trip experiences.

slides.html:
Rules of thumb

Every request gets an answer.

A no with a reason builds more trust than silence. So does "not now, and we won't follow up."

Meet the requester before a large request goes in the log.

Most arrive as solutions. The problem underneath is usually smaller or different.

Small requests belong to the product owner.

If the product manager is ordering the board, the bucket has turned into a second roadmap.

Don't score requests at triage.

Scoring models and 2x2s belong at planning, not in a 45-minute weekly meeting.

Roadmap goals are about the people the service exists for.

Editors and staff matter, and most of their asks are small fixes.

Patterns go up, requests stay put.

Twelve requests about the same problem make one idea. The twelve stay small requests.
